extracted.intended_audience: artists, glassmakers, stained-glass designers, architects, and students of art/architecture
extracted.subtask_description: Normative principles for designing and evaluating works in architecture, sculpture, and glass, emphasizing fidelity to material properties, structural honesty, and appropriate aesthetic aims (with specific guidance for glassmaking and shafts in Venetian architecture).

rubrics_metrics.name: Material-specific aims
rubrics_metrics.description: All art, working with given materials, must propose to itself the objects which, with those materials, are most perfectly attainable; and becomes illegitimate and debased if it propose to itself any other objects, better attainable with other materials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose ends that the chosen material naturally and perfectly attains. Examples: intricate ramification and detached folds are good aims for painting and metalwork, but are illegitimate as chief ends for sculpture. The principle underlies later specific rules about sculpture, glass, and windows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sculptural restraint on intricate detail
rubrics_metrics.description: Sculpture should not profess as its chief end the expression of extreme slenderness, lightness, or intricate fibrous structure (e.g., a bird's nest).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If such forms are required, represent only the general form and only as much of the fibrous structure as can be executed with perfect ease in the material; attempting full realistic carving of such delicate textures is 'debased' and physically impracticable (example: carving a bird's nest out of marble).

rubrics_metrics.name: Honor and exhibit material qualities
rubrics_metrics.description: The workman must 'honour' the materials by bringing out their particular beauties: exhibit marble's transparency and solidity, iron's strength and tenacity, gold's ductility, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design and execution should praise the material's inherent virtues rather than disguise them; aim to recommend and exalt the peculiar qualities of the substance used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Glass vessels must proclaim ductility
rubrics_metrics.description: When glass is used for vessels, the work should loudly proclaim its ductility when heated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid cut glass and over-finished precision that conceal the material's malleability; prefer forms showing blowing/moulding spontaneity—wild, extravagant, grotesque grace rather than refined, painfully finished shapes. Practical guidance: no workman ought to spend more than an hour making any glass vessel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Glass windows must proclaim transparency and color
rubrics_metrics.description: When glass is employed for windows, its chief virtues are transparency and susceptibility of brilliant color; works should emphasize these qualities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not attempt pictorial painting that makes the window a 'pretty picture'—that obscures transparency and inverts natural light/colour relations. Instead aim for serene, intense, brilliant harmonies, with easily legible and quaint subjects; treat the window like 'flaming jewellery' rather than an oil-paint picture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Against cut glass
rubrics_metrics.description: All cut glass is 'barbarous' because cutting conceals ductility and confuses glass with crystal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid cutting and over-precise finishing in glasswork; favour techniques that reveal blowing/moulding and the unique appearance of glass.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid pictorial stained-glass (windows-as-pictures)
rubrics_metrics.description: Turning painted windows into pretty pictures is a gross and ridiculous barbarism that injures appreciation of both painting and glass.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pictorial treatment (oil-ground, opacity in lights) reverses natural conditions and defeats both media: painted windows will destroy appreciation of pictorial color and obscure the transparency that is the spiritual and aesthetic strength of glass windows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideal qualities of painted windows
rubrics_metrics.description: The true perfection of a painted window is to be serene, intense, brilliant (like flaming jewellery), full of easily legible and quaint subjects, and exquisitely subtle yet simple in its harmonies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use brilliant, pure color, clear simple scenes/symbols, and restrained complexity; the author cites twelfth- and thirteenth-century French windows as consummations of this ideal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confess fragility and avoid wasting art on daily-use glass
rubrics_metrics.description: Be honest about glass's fragility; do not waste 'real art' on objects intended for daily use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because glass is fragile and liable to imperfection, do not spend excessive time or costly refinement on everyday glass vessels; workmanship should be appropriate to the material's practical role.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use wall proximity to display shaft color and texture
rubrics_metrics.description: Placing a wall veil close behind shafts enhances their color and quality by producing sharp shadows and subtle half-shadows that bring out brilliancy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design façades so shafts stand within a few inches of the sheeting behind them to create sharp relief in sunlight; this arrangement maximizes the visual display of the shaft's material (as at St. Mark's).

rubrics_metrics.name: Expose structural honesty of shafts
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not make shafts appear to perform more structural work than they actually do; show their true role.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leave many shafts visibly with half their capitals projecting beyond the archivolts they sustain to indicate the wall's partial independence; avoid dishonest visual claims that columns bear full loads when they do not.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper superimposition of shafts (diminution and multiplication)
rubrics_metrics.description: Superimposition of shafts should diminish size and increase number upward (upper shafts smaller and more numerous), the only 'right' kind of shaft superimposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This principle, analogous to tree-structure, provides structural logic and beauty; criticizes Renaissance practice of stacking identical shafts and architects who call proper subdivision 'against law.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance-based structural design
rubrics_metrics.description: Some architectural points (e.g., portico corners) depend on accuracy of poise and balanced disposition of weights rather than broad foundations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Express balance in design elements (e.g., a shaft with a different, higher base and circular rather than square plinth, set obliquely) to indicate reliance on poise not grasp; design should communicate the intended structural concept.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allocate shaft sizes functionally
rubrics_metrics.description: Use available shafts of varying sizes for appropriate functions: largest for nave shafts, smallest for windows, jambs, balustrades, niches, etc.; middle-sized sorted into classes for different stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select and place shafts according to their available size and strength, turning part of the wall veil into shaft where necessary so as not to pretend unsupported capability in small shafts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid gratuitous decorative shafts
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not introduce small satellitic shafts purely for theoretical or gratuitous ornament where they have no intrinsic constructive value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decorative elements should have intrinsic beauty or legitimate structural/visual function; criticizes early English piers where small shafts are introduced without excuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dress as social and moral design
rubrics_metrics.description: Design of dress can and should express social aims—Venetian dress was invented to promote equality, modesty, religious gravity, and peace.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clothing form (long, not convenient for quick temperaments) was chosen to signal civic virtues; consider external signs of communal values when designing dress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stained-glass color as spiritual sign
rubrics_metrics.description: The transparency and brilliance of coloured glass in church windows carries a spiritual typification (entrances of the Holy Spirit) and must be preserved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid pictorial opacity that conceals color; keep windows vivid, pure in hue, and symbolically luminous so they fulfill both aesthetic and spiritual functions.
